Key Drivers of Future Energy Demand
M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
Lesson 1 Overview
This lesson explores the major trends and structural shifts shaping the future of global energy demand.

It examines how demographic changes, urbanization, industrialization, rising middle-class consumption, and climate impacts are influencing energy use across sectors and regions.

The lesson also highlights the dual role of technology, electrification, and digitalization as both enablers of efficiency and drivers of new demand.
By understanding these interconnected forces, learners will gain the analytical tools needed to anticipate future energy needs and support inclusive, forward-looking energy planning.
M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
A: Status of Future Energy Demand

Projecting the future of global energy demand is a complex task that requires a deep understanding of the physical characteristics of energy systems, as well as the dynamic factors influencing demand and production such as economic growth, population trends, urbanization, and technological innovation.

While the future cannot be predicted with precision, leading energy institutions develop scenarios based on carefully crafted assumptions that provide plausible pathways for how energy demand may evolve.
In its World Energy Outlook 2024, the IEA outlines three main scenarios to present the future of energy demand.
In the Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS), which reflects current policies and regulations, global energy demand continues to grow.
Global primary energy demand increases by 6% from 640 exajoules (EJ) in 2023 to over 680 EJ by 2035, and reaching 740 EJ in 2050, a 15% increase from 2023.

This trajectory assumes continued economic growth (around 3% per year globally) and a decline in energy intensity, meaning the amount of energy used to produce a given level of output, a signal that energy systems are getting more efficient.
Notably, fossil fuels are projected to shrink from 80% of the global energy mix in 2023 to 58% in 2050, while clean energy sources grow rapidly.

In contrast, the Announced Pledges Scenario (APS) imagines a future where current climate and energy commitments across the world are fully implemented.
This scenario assumes that clean energy meets 40% of global energy demand by 2035, rising to nearly 75% by 2050.
In this context, global energy demand decreases continuously to reach 625 EJ in 2035 and 610 EJ in 2050, reaching levels 4.7% inferior to 2023.

The slowdown is largely due to accelerated <ai prompt="What is energy efficiency?">energy efficiency 💬️</ai> measures and expanded electrification in end-use sectors such as transport, buildings, and industry.
The most ambitious pathway, the Net Zero Emissions (NZE) Scenario, aligns with limiting global warming to 1.5°C.
It assumes that 90% of global energy demand will be met by clean energy by 2050, and that any remaining fossil fuel use will be offset or abated.
In this scenario, total energy demand declines by 16% by 2035, and continues to fall through mid-century.
This reduction would take place despite economic and population growth, driven by deep efficiency gains, behavioral change, and structural transformations.
“In all our scenarios, growth in global energy demand slows thanks to efficiency gains, electrification and a rapid buildout of renewables.”
IEA, World Energy Outlook, 2024
However, not all analyses project a decline in energy demand.
According to a 2023 McKinsey report, global energy demand may grow faster than previously expected, depending on geopolitical and economic developments.
Their projections vary from an 11% increase in demand by 2050 from 2023 levels in the “Continued Momentum” scenario to an 18% increase in the “Slow Evolution” case.
Emerging economies account for most of this growth, as population growth and rising incomes are projected to drive much of the additional demand.
Taken together, these outlooks show that future energy demand is not predetermined.
It depends on policy choices, innovation trajectories, and global coordination.
While trends like population growth, urbanization, and geopolitics may increase demand, technologies such as efficiency improvements and electrification can help curb it.

IRENA offers a complementary perspective in its 2024 World Energy Transitions Outlook, this time looking at the total final energy consumption that measured the energy delivered and used by end consumers, as opposed to the total energy required by the system (energy demand).
IRENA’s 1.5°C Scenario projects a 10% reduction in total final energy consumption by 2050, relative to today’s levels.

This also supposes that the share of electricity in final energy consumption must increase from 23% in 2022 to 52% by 2050, supported by widespread adoption of electric vehicles, heat pumps, and renewable-powered industrial applications.
Renewable energy’s share of final consumption needs to rise to 35% by 2030 and 78% by 2050, up from 17% in 2022.

B: Population Growth and Demographic Shifts

Population growth is an important factor of future energy demand, although the rate of this growth is slowing down from 2% of annual average growth rate in the 1960’s to less than 1% today ((UNDESA, 2024).
From 8.2 billion in 2024, the global population is expected to reach 8.5 billion by 2030, 9.7 billion by 2050, and peak at around 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s before gradually declining.
But the trend is not uniform across the globe as Global North and Global South exhibit different trajectories.
In 63 countries, home to 28% of the world’s population, including China, Germany, Japan, and Russia, populations are in decline.
By contrast, 126 countries, mostly in sub-Saharan Africa and parts of Asia, are projected to see their populations continue to grow through 2054.
These regions are expected to see a 38% population increase, while declining regions face a 14% decrease.
This divergence has major implications for energy demand.

Rapidly growing populations in countries like Angola, Niger, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Central African Republic, and Somalia—all projected to double in size between 2024 and 2054—will require massive expansions in energy infrastructure and services.
Most of the countries and areas facing rapid population growth over the next decades are classified today as “low-income economies”.
They will need to increase their energy consumption substantially if they are to develop economically and achieve the Goals and targets of the 2030 Agenda.
UNDESA, 2024

In contrast, countries with slow growth, such as Brazil, Viet Nam, and Iran, will have a more gradual increase in energy needs, offering opportunities to invest in efficiency and low-carbon transitions with less demographic pressure.

Meanwhile, countries with declining populations, such as China which is projected to lose 204 million people by 2054, may see their total energy demand plateau or shrink, though this will be shaped by urban density, industrial activity, and aging-related shifts in consumption patterns.
Demographic dynamics are reshaping the geography of energy demand.
As growth concentrates in the Global South, where access gaps remain wide, and populations decline in energy-intensive economies, the global energy map will need to adjust.
Planning for the future of energy means anticipating technological and economic shifts while aligning them with the evolving realities of where people live, grow, and age.

C: Urbanization and Industrialization
The world’s cities are growing.
Today, 55% of the world’s population live in urban areas, and that number is expected to increase to 68% by 2050 (UNDESA, 2024).
More strikingly, 98% of global population growth (IRENA, 2024) will take place in emerging markets and developing economies.

This is expected to significantly contribute to energy demand surge in these regions as urban living brings higher per capita energy consumption, driven by lighting, appliances, mobility, and more critically cooling.
In rapidly urbanizing regions, demand for residential cooling is expected to triple by 2050, rising from 2.6 EJ to 7.7 EJ in the APS scenario from the IEA (IEA, 2024).
By then, space cooling alone will account for 14% of total building energy demand, up from just 7% today.
This transformation is particularly striking in the Global South.
Electricity use in buildings is projected to grow from 37% of building energy demand in 2023 to over 50% by 2050, adding more than 35 EJ, mostly in emerging economies.
Powering growing cities

While cities increasingly shape the future of livelihoods, industry remains the world’s largest energy consumer, responsible for 39 % of total global final energy consumption in 2023 and nearly half of all energy-related CO₂ emissions (IEA,2024).

Much of this is concentrated in emerging economies: In 2012, non‑OECD countries accounted for 67% of the world's industrial energy consumption, and this share is projected to increase to 73% by 2040 (EIA, 2016)

Industrial energy demand grew by 2% in 2023 alone, driven by sectors like steel, cement, and chemicals.
These industries remain deeply reliant on fossil fuels, especially coal and natural gas, to supply high-temperature heat.
However, this trend begins to shift after 2030 in climate-aligned scenarios.
In the APS, electricity’s share in industrial energy use increases from 22% in 2023 to 27% by 2030, with China contributing more than half of this growth (IEA, 2024).
IRENA’s 1.5°C scenario shows an even more pronounced shift, projecting 36% electrification of industry by 2050, with large-scale deployment of hydrogen and heat pumps (IRENA,2024) .
Together, urbanization and industrialization are reshaping the future of energy demand.
These factors raise new challenges for <ai prompt="Explain decarbonization.">decarbonization 💬️</ai>, but also present new opportunities for innovation, job creation, and inclusive development.

D: Rising Middle Class
Rising Middle Class and Lifestyle Changes
As the global economy continues to expand, particularly across emerging markets, populations are changing the way they consume energy.
One major drive for this transformation is the rapid growth of the middle class.
Between 2024 and 2034, the number of middle-class households in emerging markets is expected to nearly double, from 354 million to 687 million (Oxford Economics, 2024).
Asia-Pacific is the epicenter of this transformation.
By 2029, two out of every three middle-class households in emerging markets will be located in that region.
China will remain the largest market, home to 300 million middle-class households by 2034, representing 44% of the total (Oxford Economics, 2024).
India’s middle class, meanwhile, will more than double from 27 million households in 2024 to 62 million by 2029, becoming the second-largest globally.
“We expect the emerging markets middle class to double in the next decade – expanding from 354 million households in 2024 to 687 million households by 2034..”
Oxford Economics, 2024
As incomes rise, so does the appetite for energy-intensive goods: more air conditioners, refrigerators, personal vehicles, and digital devices.

According to the IEA, by 2035, rising incomes and warmer temperatures are projected to add 1,200 TWh of electricity demand for cooling, which is more than the current electricity use of the entire Middle East (IEA, 2024).
In the building sector alone, nearly 45% of electricity demand growth through 2035 will come from increased consumption mostly driven by middle-class lifestyles.
But there are nuances to this rise.
While per capita income in China is expected to double to $26,000/year by 2034, India’s fast-growing middle class will still consume less than half that amount (Oxford Economics, 2024).
At the same time, households in emerging markets continue to spend around 10% of their disposable income on energy, making them vulnerable to price volatility and potentially tempering consumption.
Despite these changes, overall energy demand is rising more slowly than in previous decades, thanks to improvements in energy efficiency and the spread of electrification.
Global GDP is projected to grow by 3% annually between 2023 and 2035 (IEA, 2024) but energy demand is increasing at a much lower rate.
This decoupling reflects a shift in the global energy landscape, where demand is shaped not just by how many people consume energy, but by how, where, and what they consume.

E: Electrification of End-Use and hard to abate Sectors

Electrification is emerging as a major force in the global energy sector and is projected to become the world’s largest energy source by 2050.

According to one analysis by the global consulting firm McKinsey, electricity consumption could more than double under slower energy transition scenarios and nearly triple in faster ones.

This increase is fueled by traditional sectors like buildings and appliances but also increasingly by newer and fast-growing demands such as data centers, battery electric vehicles (BEVs), and hydrogen production.

For example, global green hydrogen consumption is expected to rise from less than 1 Mtpa today to 179 Mtpa by 2050, contributing to about 20% annual growth in power demand for the sector (McKinsey, 2024).

Electricity demand from transport alone is projected to grow by 10% annually, with BEVs expected to account for the majority of global passenger car sales by 2050, up from just 13% today (McKinsey, 2024).

In buildings, heating and cooling 💬️ are becoming increasingly electrified.

By 2050, the world could see the deployment of 793 million heat pump units and 2.2 billion electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles (IRENA, 2024).

Electrification is also transforming industry, including hard-to-abate sectors.
In China, for example, 60% of electricity is consumed by industry, which is twice the OECD average and accounted for 48% of total demand growth between 2022 and 2024 (IEA, 2025).

Electrification of clean tech supply chains is also intensifying in 2024 alone, the production of solar panels, batteries, and EVs used 320 TWh of electricity, equivalent to Italy’s entire annual electricity use.
Even when we look at the near future, global electricity demand is expected to increase by 3,500 TWh between 2025 and 2027, equivalent to adding the electricity demand of Japan each year (IEA, 2025).
Smart electrification solutions will be essential to navigate this transformation.
Smart electrification solutions can reduce peak electricity demand by up to 50% and cut network losses by up to 63%, helping to manage growing power needs more efficiently (IRENA, 2024).
The acceleration of electrification is expected to be powered by low-emission sources.
According to the IEA, 95% of the rise in global electricity demand is expected to be met by renewables by 2027, particularly solar and wind.
It’s important to note that emerging and developing economies are expected to account for 85% of this demand growth, with China alone contributing over 50% (IEA, 2025).
With the right policies and investments, electrification can be a powerful tool to decarbonize economies while improving energy access.

F: Digitalization and AI-driven demand growth

Digitalization and AI are expected to become significant drivers of the future of global energy demand. As electricity emerges as the dominant energy carrier by 2050, consumption will arise from traditional sectors such as the electrification of homes and factories, but also from the vast digital infrastructure behind the AI revolution.
Among the most energy-intensive elements of this transformation are data centers.
Globally, these facilities consumed 415 TWh of electricity in 2024 (IEA, 2025), accounting for 1.5% of total electricity use.
By 2030, this figure is expected to more than double to 945 TWh, exceeding the entire current electricity consumption of Japan.
Looking further ahead, McKinsey estimates that by 2050, electricity demand from data centers could range from 2,500 to 4,500 TWh, representing 5% to 9% of global electricity demand (McKinsey, 2024).
This rise will come from not cloud computing and cryptocurrency, but especially from the energy-hungry processes required for AI model training and generative ai 💬️ applications like ChatGPT.
Some of the largest data centers under construction today are expected to consume as much electricity as 2 million households (IEA, 2025).
Renewables are expected to provide the largest contribution to meet data center demand, rising to 450TW by 2035 according to the IEA.
But dispatchable sources like natural gas and nuclear will also play a critical role in powering this infrastructure.

As energy infrastructure races to keep up with the AI revolution, technical challenges will arise with 20% (IEA, 2025) of planned data centers likely to face delays due to grid congestion and equipment shortages.
Despite this pressure on energy consumption, digitalization and AI also offer powerful tools to improve the efficiency of energy systems.

Smart technologies, such as AI-enabled forecasting, grid optimization, and fault detection, could unlock 175 GW of additional grid capacity and reduce electricity consumption in buildings by 300 TWh, equivalent to the entire electricity generation of Australia and New Zealand (IEA, 2025).
At the city level, digital tools can help reduce renewable curtailment by more than 25%, improve system efficiency by 30%, and cut customer costs by up to 30% (IEA, 2024).
Integrated urban planning powered by AI, combined with smart meters, sensors, and real-time data, can help cities balance loads, manage peak demand, and build resilience.
However, beyond technology, realizing the full benefits of digitalization will require investment in digital skills, data governance, and supportive regulation.

As digital and AI systems increasingly influence how and where energy is consumed, empowering local governments with the capacity to plan, regulate, and optimize energy transitions will be essential to making digitalization a driver of sustainable and inclusive development.

G: Impact of Climate Change and Extreme Weather Events
With climate change accelerating, its effects are influencing how we produce energy, but also how much of it we will need.
Rising temperatures, a growing population, and changing weather patterns are expected to significantly increase energy demand globally, one major driver being the rise in demand for cooling.

For example, residential air-conditioning demand is expected to increase from nearly 300 TWh in 2000 to approximately 4,000 TWh by 205027, much of it in emerging economies as a consequence of rising incomes and warming climates.
Cooking practices and other household energy needs are also likely to become more electricity intensive.
At the same time, energy systems themselves face increasing risks.
Thermal power plants risk efficiency loss in the future as temperatures rise and water availability declines.
Hydropower could be affected by changes in rainfall patterns and higher evaporation rates, with projections showing, for example, a 35% reduction in Zambezi River basin hydropower capacity by 2050.

Meanwhile, stronger storms, floods, and extreme heat expose energy infrastructure to growing threats such as damaged transmission lines and disrupted pipelines which compromise the safe operation of energy facilities.
These risks demand urgent adaptation to ensure energy system resilience.

For a deeper exploration of how to build climate-resilient and adaptive energy systems, please consult Module 6 of the Sustainable Energy Academy, which is dedicated to climate impacts, adaptation strategies, and the intersection between energy and resilience.
Key Takeaways

Energy demand will be shaped by structural drivers including population growth, urbanization, industrialization, and the rise of a global middle classparticularly in emerging economies where infrastructure and consumption are rapidly expanding.

Technology plays a dual role: electrification and digitalization are driving new sources of energy demand (data centers, electric vehicles), while also enabling greater efficiency, flexibility, and system optimization.

The future of energy demand is not fixed; it will depend on policy decisions, innovation, and global cooperation to align demographic, economic, and technological trends with sustainability and equity goals.
